title: fix(fields): LocationField's fallback placeholder speaks the reader's language (objectui#8149)
body:
Fixes #8149
Clause-②: no

When a `location` field declares no `placeholder`, `LocationField` showed the English literal `latitude, longitude`. objectui#6888 had already keyed the two coordinate nouns (`fields.location.latitude` / `fields.location.longitude`) for the residue refusal, so on a zh console the box said `latitude` while the refusal one line beneath it said 纬度: the same word, twice, in two languages.

## The decision, stated so it can be audited

This extends objectui#6755's principle (a widget's own copy is keyed) to placeholder copy, as the claim comment `5826637663` states. The authored `field.placeholder` still wins, verbatim, in every language; only the fallback changes.

⚠️ One precedent reads differently on `main` than the triage grading and the claim cite it. objectui#4028 keyed `AddressField`'s five sub-labels, but it **dropped** the five placeholders rather than keying them; the reasoning is the comment above the sub-inputs in `AddressField.tsx`. Its first criterion is the one that matters here: a placeholder earns its place when it "teaches a FORMAT its label cannot". `latitude, longitude` is exactly that (the order and the separator this box parses), and objectui#4028's other two reasons do not apply here: the right example there depends on the address's country, while the coordinate format is the same everywhere; and keying there cost invented example data in ten packs, while this change adds no pack entry at all. So objectui#4028 supports this change on its own criterion, and objectui#3342 (`TagsField`'s placeholder, keyed) is the direct affirmative precedent.

## What moved

- `packages/fields/src/widgets/LocationField.tsx`: a new `placeholderPair(t)` joins `coordinateName(t, 'latitude')` and `coordinateName(t, 'longitude')`, the same two noun keys the residue refusal names a half with, in `COORDINATE_LABELS` order, with an ASCII `, `. The input reads `config?.placeholder || placeholderPair(t)`.
- **No new keys.** `useFieldTranslation.ts` and the ten locale packs are untouched; every pack already carries both nouns.
- The component docblock's sentence ending "which is why the placeholder is unchanged" now says what it was about: the objectui#6272 storage rename (the placeholder names the coordinates, not the `lat` / `lng` keys). It also says outright that this is a statement about key names, not about language, so it cannot be read as a translation ruling.
- Stored `{ lat, lng }` handling and the retired `{ latitude, longitude }` handling are untouched.

## The separator: why the widget owns it, not the packs

⚠️ **This departs from one phrase of the claim because of a measurement, and says so openly.** The claim's scope says "The separator is the locale's business. Read how objectui#8148 settled the comma-decimal concern before choosing it." Having read it, I did not hand the separator to the packs, so the dispatch's preferred shape (a locale-owned joiner key) was not taken. The reasons:

- In this placeholder the separator is **input grammar**, not punctuation. `parseDraft` splits the typed text on an ASCII `,` and reads the first part as the latitude. A pack-owned joiner (the `validation.formInvalidJoiner` shape) or a pair value like `{{latitude}}, {{longitude}}` would let a pack write its own script's comma: U+FF0C FULLWIDTH COMMA in zh, U+3001 IDEOGRAPHIC COMMA in ja, U+060C ARABIC COMMA in ar. **Measured:** a pair typed with each of those three is refused (format refusal, `onChange` not called, `aria-invalid="true"`), while the same pair with an ASCII comma is accepted. So a pack-owned separator could make the hint teach a format this box refuses. A pair value would also hand the pack the ORDER, which the parser owns too.
- objectui#8148 handled the comma-decimal concern the same way: the widget fills in the example digits in ASCII, so no pack spells a digit and the collision "cannot occur rather than being avoided by good behaviour" (its PR, #9869). Here no pack spells the separator.
- The translators had already made the same choice. Every pack's `fields.location.refusedFormat` example is written `30.2741, 120.1551` with the ASCII separator (pinned per pack below). Where a pack names the noun pair with a comma in its prose, it is the ASCII one too: zh writes 纬度, 经度, not its prose comma.

What remains the locale's business is the words. If the maintainer wants a pack-owned separator anyway, it costs one joiner key in every pack plus a pin that every value's separator is the ASCII comma, so the only thing a pack could change is the whitespace. This is listed as an open question in the report on the card.

## The pin, and what it measured

`packages/fields/src/__tests__/LocationField.placeholderI18n-8149.test.tsx` (33 cases) plus `LocationField.placeholder.no-provider-8149.test.tsx` (3 cases). The provider-less leg is its own file for the reason `TagsField.placeholder.no-provider.test.tsx` states: mounting `I18nProvider` installs a global react-i18next instance, after which no provider-less state is observable in that module graph.

- The claim's rows: under `zh-CN` (and `zh`) the placeholder is `纬度, 经度` with no English noun left; under `en` it is `latitude, longitude`; an authored placeholder wins under both `en` and `zh-CN`.
- The card's own shape: under `zh-CN`, the placeholder's first noun is the word the residue refusal beneath it uses.
- The separator measurement above (three refusals plus the ASCII positive control).
- Every pack, with the population read off `builtInLocales` itself: the rendered hint, split the way `parseDraft` splits, is that pack's latitude noun then its longitude noun. Each pack's `refusedFormat` example also uses the same separator.
- Control: under `zh` and `zh-CN`, `AddressField` renders its translated labels (keyed by objectui#4028) in the same run, so a dead provider cannot make the negative assertions pass.
- No provider: `latitude, longitude`, no raw key, no CJK shipped from code, and the authored placeholder wins.

**Ablation at `36c090e1d` (the final head).** The English literal was put back through `ablation-replace.mjs`:

- anchor hits went 1 → 0, and the blob went `f3dc943bfdf5` → `fa8c9b1feba0`;
- on-disk counts: new call 1 → 0, literal 0 → 1;
- the restore from `HEAD` brought the blob back to `f3dc943bfdf5`, equal to the `HEAD` blob, with `git diff HEAD` empty.

```
Tests  10 failed | 26 passed (36)
```

The 10 reds are exactly the defect:

- `zh-CN` and `zh`;
- the same-word row;
- the per-pack split for the seven packs whose nouns differ from English: zh, ja, ko, de, es, ru and ar.

These stayed green on both sides:

- the authored-placeholder rows and `en`;
- the `fr` / `pt` / `en` per-pack rows (their nouns ARE `latitude` / `longitude`);
- the separator measurements, the `refusedFormat` rows and the control;
- the provider-less file.

After the restore, the two files are 36 / 36.

## Changeset

`.changeset/8149-location-placeholder-localized.md`: `'@object-ui/fields': patch` (visible copy only, no contract change).

## Acceptance notes

Noted, not filed:

- `content/docs/fields/location.mdx` and `examples/schema-catalog/src/schemas/fields-location/basic-location-field.json` both author `placeholder: 'latitude, longitude'`. The runtime shows an authored placeholder verbatim, so an app that copies the example now pins English over the localized fallback. Class (c) excludes metadata the runtime honours but that makes the result worse, so this is recorded here as a boundary case. Carrier: none.
- `packages/app-shell/src/utils/paramValueShape.ts` describes `location` (and `geolocation`) as a `{ latitude, longitude }` object in its `note` prose; objectui#6272 retired that spelling for `location`. Only `base` and `cardinality` are asserted, and nothing reads the `note` prose. Carrier: none.
- Dispatch premise refinements: the defaults map is `packages/fields/src/widgets/useFieldTranslation.ts` (not under `hooks/`), and the objectui#4028 precedent reads as described above.
